question: What does drug non-compliance mean in nursing practice?

options.A: A doctor writing an illegible prescription slip
options.B: A nurse administering the wrong dose of medication
options.C: A pharmacy running out of essential prescribed drugs
options.D: A patient failing to follow a prescribed medication regimen

explanation: Non-compliance simply means the patient is not taking their drugs the way the doctor or nurse instructed them to. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which behavior is a clear sign of medication non-adherence?

options.A: Asking the pharmacist about the cost of a new drug
options.B: Taking a morning pill one hour earlier than usual
options.C: Reporting a mild side effect to the attending nurse
options.D: Stopping a blood pressure pill because the patient feels better

explanation: Stopping medication simply because symptoms disappear shows a lack of adherence to the long-term treatment plan. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h1)

question: The main reason a patient with high blood pressure might stop taking their medication is that...

options.A: blood pressure pills must only be taken for one week
options.B: the condition usually causes no daily physical symptoms
options.C: pharmacies always keep drug prices extremely low

explanation: Because high blood pressure is often a silent killer, patients feel fine and mistakenly assume they do not need their daily pills. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h2)

question: A patient taking five different medications at different times of the day is most likely to experience non-compliance due to...

options.A: complete absence of any possible side effects
options.B: excessive financial savings from bulk buying
options.C: immediate physical healing from all conditions
options.D: a confusing and overwhelming pill schedule

explanation: Complex drug regimens with multiple timings cause heavy fatigue and confusion, making it very easy to miss doses. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is a direct clinical result of long-term drug non-compliance in chronic illnesses?

options.A: Immediate and permanent cure of the medical condition
options.B: Worsening of the disease and potential organ damage
options.C: Stable laboratory test results over many months
options.D: Strengthening of the immune system against infections

explanation: Without steady medication, chronic diseases progress unchecked, eventually destroying vital organs like the heart and kidneys. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h3)

question: A patient with heart failure repeatedly misses their diuretic medication. What is this patient most likely to experience?

options.A: Severe fluid overload and breathing difficulties
options.B: Lowered blood pressure to normal limits
options.C: Complete recovery from heart muscle weakness
options.D: Rapid weight loss and extreme dehydration

explanation: Diuretics help the body get rid of excess fluid; missing them allows fluid to back up into the lungs, causing severe shortness of breath. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h3)

question: Why does stopping antibiotics early lead to drug resistance?

options.A: The body becomes immune to the healing power of rest
options.B: Expired medications lose their chemical composition
options.C: Stronger bacteria survive low drug levels and multiply
options.D: Good bacteria in the gut destroy the remaining pills

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early leaves the toughest germs alive, and they multiply to create strains that the drug can no longer kill. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which outcome is associated with treatment failure caused by drug resistance?

options.A: Bacterial infections disappear without any medical care
options.B: Medical costs and hospital stays decrease significantly
options.C: Infections become harder to treat with standard drugs
options.D: Patients recover much faster from common illnesses

explanation: When microbes become resistant, routine medications fail, forcing doctors to use stronger, more toxic, and costlier therapies. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h4)

question: What dangerous habit is a common form of erratic medication non-compliance?

options.A: Reporting mild nausea directly to the attending nurse
options.B: Consulting a pharmacist before changing a schedule
options.C: Storing prescription drugs in a cool, dry cupboard
options.D: Taking a double dose to makeup for a missed pill

explanation: Patients often try to compensate for a forgotten pill by taking two at the next scheduled time, which risks drug toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h5)

question: How does erratic drug dosing directly affect a patient's body?

options.A: It stabilizes blood pressure within normal ranges
options.B: It helps the liver filter out toxins much faster
options.C: It ensures steady healing and faster tissue repair
options.D: It causes dangerous blood levels leading to toxicity

explanation: Unpredictable timing and dosing create wild spikes in drug concentration, pushing safe levels into toxic territory. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following is an indirect method to assess medication adherence?

options.A: Checking tissue biopsies for microscopic drug deposits
options.B: Analyzing urine specimens for active chemical traces
options.C: Counting the remaining pills in the medicine bottle
options.D: Measuring exact drug metabolites in a blood sample

explanation: Pill counts, patient interviews, and refill records are indirect ways to check compliance without laboratory drug assays. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why should nurses avoid relying solely on a patient's verbal report about taking their medications?

options.A: Patients often claim they take pills even when they miss them
options.B: Patients never remember the names of their prescribed drugs
options.C: Verbal reports are illegal to record in hospital charts
options.D: Doctors prefer laboratory tests over talking to patients

explanation: Patients want to please their healthcare providers and often say they take their medications faithfully when they actually do not. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h6)

question: What practical tool can a nurse recommend to help an elderly patient who forgets daily doses?

options.C: A large wall calendar for appointments

explanation: Pill boxes sorted by day and time help patients easily see whether they have taken their scheduled medications. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h7)

question: A patient struggles to understand a complicated medication schedule with four different drugs. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient to double the morning dose instead
options.B: Scold the patient for being careless with prescriptions
options.C: Stop all the medications until the patient feels better
options.D: Work with the doctor to simplify the dosing schedule

explanation: Simplifying complex regimens reduces confusion and makes it much easier for the patient to follow the treatment plan. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h7)
